references.text: Describes the beginning of the Israelites' forced labor under Egyptian taskmasters, leading to the bitter oppression mentioned in verse 14.
The Israelites groaned under slavery and cried out to God, a direct result of the hard work described in 1:14.
Pharaoh increases the workload with bricks and straw, elaborating on the hard labor with clay and bricks mentioned in 1:14.
God promises to free the Israelites from the harsh forced labor (בְּפָרֶךְ) imposed upon them.
Uses the same word for harshness (בְּפָרֶךְ) and forbids Israelites from treating one another as the Egyptians treated them.
Repeats the prohibition against ruling with harshness (בְּפָרֶךְ), a direct reference to Egyptian oppression.
A historical reflection on the Egyptians' oppression and the hard labor they imposed on the Israelites.
The psalm recalls deliverance from forced labor, where shoulders were freed from the burden and hands from the baskets.
Ezekiel uses the same expression (בְּפָרֶךְ) to criticize leaders who rule harshly over the people.
Stephen's speech refers to how the Egyptians mistreated the Israelites' ancestors and forced them to expose their infants.
God says He has seen His people's suffering in Egypt, a reference to the oppression described in Exodus 1:14.
Hebrews 11:37 summarizes the historical suffering described in Exodus as part of the fate of the heroes of faith.
Thematic parallel: Oppression in Exodus (external) versus oppression in Micah (internal), highlighting God's hatred of injustice regardless of who commits it.
